after: ## From using a source to synthesising sources
alt: Three sources with a few relevant lines highlighted feed a funnel that selects the most relevant information and combines apt, specific material into the writer’s own argument. A note reminds that some sources are more credible than others.
caption: Synthesis selects from several sources and combines them in service of your claim.

alt: Three summary sentences each begin “Source A says”, “Source B says”, “Source C says”. The synthesis sentence begins with the issue, whether a car park should become green space, and brings in the survey, the shopkeeper and the planner as evidence. A table compares organising principle, relationship, commentary and selection.
caption: In synthesis the claim is the subject of the sentence; the sources are the evidence.

after: ## Ways of bringing source material in
alt: Quotation, paraphrase and summary, each with when to use it and an example from the fictional sources: the shopkeeper’s “trees don’t buy bread”, his point about customers spending about £40, and the planner’s account of a northern town. Below, signal verbs and a warning about dropped quotes.
caption: Quote for force, paraphrase a point, summarise a passage: always attribute and comment.

alt: Four cards with small diagrams: agreement (two sources point to one idea), extension (one source adds to another), qualification (one source limits another) and conflict (two sources disagree), each with example phrasing.
caption: Agree, extend, qualify or conflict: say how the sources relate.

after: ## Worked example 1: building a synthesis paragraph
alt: The worked paragraph’s sources in order: Source A, the council survey (62% want green space), supports the claim; Source B, the shopkeeper’s letter about village visitors spending around £40, qualifies A; Source C, the planner’s article on seating and signs, extends B and supplies a remedy. They lead to a qualified claim.
caption: Order by idea: support, then qualify, then extend toward the claim.
